blocks.text: A bracket drawn by a European design office arrives at a US machine shop. The shop reads the top view as if it were a bottom view and cuts the slot on the wrong face. Nothing was misdrawn: the two offices used different projection systems and the symbol that told them so was ignored.

blocks.markdown: A three-dimensional part is described on paper by **orthographic projection**: looking straight at it along an axis and drawing what you see, repeated from several directions. The usual set is the **front view**, the **top (plan) view** and a **side view**. How these views are arranged on the sheet depends on the projection system, **first angle** (common in Europe and under ISO) or **third angle** (common in the USA under ASME, and increasingly in ISO drawings too).

blocks.title: First and third angle
blocks.text: Imagine the part in a transparent box. In **third-angle** projection the viewing planes lie between the observer and the part, so each view is drawn on the near side: the **top view is above the front view** and the **right-side view is to the right of the front view**. In **first-angle** projection the part lies between the observer and the planes, so each view appears on the far side: the **top view is below the front view** and the **right-side view is to the left of the front view**.

blocks.caption: Where each view goes relative to the front view

blocks.markdown: The **projection symbol** in or near the title block tells the reader which system applies. It is a truncated cone drawn in two views: the front view of the frustum and the circular end view. The end view stands where the left-side view would be placed in that system: to the left of the frustum for third angle and to the right of it for first angle. Never guess; always read the symbol before reading the views.

blocks.title: Three views of an L-bracket
blocks.prompt: An L-bracket has a base 80 mm wide, 50 mm deep and 10 mm thick, and a vertical upright at the back that is 80 mm wide, 10 mm thick and 40 mm tall overall. Describe the front, top and right-side views in third angle.

steps.text: Front view (looking at the front face): a rectangle 80 mm wide by 40 mm tall. A visible horizontal line at 10 mm height marks where the base front face meets the upright front face, because they lie in different planes.
Top view (placed above the front view): a rectangle 80 mm by 50 mm. A visible line 10 mm from the back edge marks the upright's top face.
Right-side view (placed to the right of the front view): an L-shaped outline 50 mm wide by 40 mm tall, showing the 10 mm thick base and the 10 mm thick upright.
Check alignment: the width 80 mm is shared by front and top; the height 40 mm is shared by front and side; the depth 50 mm is shared by top and side.

blocks.answer: Front 80 x 40 rectangle, top 80 x 50 rectangle, right side an L of 50 x 40 mm; shared dimensions line up between views.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing the minimum set of views.** Draw only the views needed to describe the part completely. A view that adds no information is clutter and a source of inconsistency. Parts with constant section often need only one view and a note: a plate with its thickness given, or a turned shaft with its diameter symbol. Prismatic parts with profile changes in two directions typically need two or three.

rows: The circle is implied by the symbol
Flat plate 60 x 40 x 5 with four holes
One view plus a thickness note
Two views: front and right side
Width from front, depth from side
Block with blind hole on top and slot on the right
blocks.caption: Typical minimum sets

blocks.title: Do we need the top view?
blocks.prompt: For the L-bracket of the first example, a draughtsman proposes front and right-side views only. Does the set describe the part fully?

steps.text: Width 80 mm and height 40 mm are read from the front view.
Depth 50 mm and the L profile are read from the right-side view.
Every feature is visible in one of these views, and no feature depends on information only the top view carries, so the set is complete.

blocks.answer: Yes: two views suffice, and the top view is redundant.

blocks.title: Fewer views, if complete
blocks.text: Choose the view that best shows the shape as the front view, and add only what is needed to remove ambiguity. Hidden lines may remove the need for a view, but too many dashed lines make a view hard to read.

items: Read the projection symbol before reading any view.
Place views by the rules of that system.
Keep shared dimensions aligned between views.
Use the fewest views that remove all ambiguity.

points: Third angle puts the top view above and the right view on the right; first angle reverses both.
The truncated-cone symbol states which system is used; read it first.
The minimum view set is the smallest number of views that completely describes the part.

questions.stem: In third-angle projection, where is the top view placed relative to the front view?
questions.explanation: Third angle places each view on the near side of the box, so the top view appears above the front view. First angle places it below.

questions.stem: In first-angle projection, where does the right-side view appear?

options.text: To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view

questions.correctOptionText: To the left of the front view

distractorRationale.c: Top view position in third angle.
distractorRationale.d: Top view position in first angle.

questions.explanation: In first angle the views fall on the far side, so the view from the right appears to the left of the front view. This is the opposite of third angle.

questions.stem: A part is 90 mm wide, 50 mm high and 35 mm deep. It is drawn in third angle with front, top and right-side views, with a 20 mm gap between views. Calculate the minimum width of sheet area needed across the front and right-side views, in mm.
questions.explanation: Width = front width 90 + gap 20 + side view width (the depth) 35 = 145 mm. The side view is as wide as the part is deep.

questions.stem: A part is 70 mm wide, 45 mm high and 30 mm deep. Drawn in third angle with a 15 mm gap, calculate the height of sheet area needed for the front view and top view stacked, in mm.
questions.explanation: Height = front height 45 + gap 15 + top view height (the depth) 30 = 90 mm. The top view has the depth as its vertical size.

questions.stem: A drawing's title block shows the projection symbol with the circular end view to the right of the frustum. Which system is it?
questions.explanation: The end view is placed where the left-side view would be in that system. A left view lies to the right of the front view in first angle.

questions.stem: A turned pin has a diameter of 12 mm and a length of 60 mm. Which is the minimum set of views?

options.text: One view with a diameter symbol

questions.correctOptionText: One view with a diameter symbol
questions.explanation: The shape is the same cylinder from every side, so one view with the diameter symbol defines it. Other views only repeat information.

questions.stem: A block has a blind hole drilled into its top, a slot cut across its right face and a stepped front. Which set of views is likely the minimum?
questions.explanation: Three features are on three different faces: the hole is visible in the top, the slot in the right side, and the step in the front. Hidden lines in fewer views would be ambiguous.

questions.stem: State the differences in view placement between first-angle and third-angle projection for the top view and right-side view, and how a reader knows which system a drawing uses.
markingGuide: Third: top above front, right-side to the right
First: top below front, right-side to the left
The symbol near the title block shows the system
Read the symbol before interpreting views
questions.explanation: A correct answer gives both placements for both views and names the symbol. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: A bracket has a base plate with two holes and a vertical web. A colleague says three views are needed. Argue for the minimum set and explain how you would test whether a view is redundant.
markingGuide: Identify the info each view provides: width, height, depth
If the other views already show a feature and every dimension, a view is redundant
Choose the front view that shows the most shape
Check all features visible without ambiguous hidden lines
Conclude two or three views as appropriate with reason
questions.explanation: Marks for argument based on information content rather than a fixed rule of three views. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: Third-angle projection places the top view above the front view.
questions.explanation: In third angle the planes lie between observer and part, so views appear on the near side. The top view lies above the front view.
